value.overview: The Pacific Golden-Plover is a long-distance migratory shorebird of the northern Pacific region. It breeds in Arctic tundra across Alaska and northeastern Siberia, then travels to wintering areas around the Pacific, including eastern and southeastern Asia, Australia, Pacific islands, and parts of western North America. It is a compact, long-legged plover that usually forages in open habitats rather than dense wetlands. In Costa Rica, it is an exceptionally rare visitor.
value.classification: The Pacific Golden-Plover belongs to the plover family Charadriidae and the genus Pluvialis. It is closely related to the American Golden-Plover, but the two are separate species.
value.identification: This medium-sized plover has a mottled back patterned in gold, brown, black, and white. Nonbreeding birds are grayish-brown above with a pale face, dark eye, and whitish underparts. Breeding adults show a stronger golden-and-black pattern, with males typically developing a black face, throat, and underparts bordered by white. The bill is short and straight, and the legs are dark. It is generally more compact and shorter-winged in appearance than the American Golden-Plover.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds on open Arctic tundra in Alaska and Siberia, especially on relatively dry, well-drained ground with low vegetation. During migration and winter it uses coastal mudflats, salt ponds, beaches, estuaries, mangroves, wet grassland, pasture, agricultural fields, and other short-grass habitats. In Costa Rica it is not a regular common migrant; it is recorded as an accidental or exceptionally rare vagrant. The first documented Costa Rican record involved a bird in winter plumage at salt ponds with other roosting shorebirds.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Most individuals leave Arctic breeding grounds after summer and travel along Pacific flyways to wintering areas. In Costa Rica, the species is an extremely rare accidental visitor rather than a predictable seasonal migrant, although suitable coastal salt ponds, mudflats, and other open shorebird habitats may occasionally attract a wandering individual.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs during the short Arctic summer. Pairs nest on the ground in open tundra, usually placing a shallow scrape among low vegetation, moss, or lichen. The clutch generally contains four eggs, which are well camouflaged against the tundra. Both adults participate in incubation and defense of the nest. Chicks are precocial and leave the nest soon after hatching, following adults while feeding themselves. After breeding, adults and young migrate south separately or in loose groups.
value.dietFeeding: Pacific Golden-Plovers feed mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, including beetles, flies, grasshoppers, worms, and mollusks. They may also take crustaceans and, in some wintering habitats, berries, seeds, or other plant material. The usual feeding method is a repeated run-and-stop sequence: the bird moves quickly, pauses to scan, and then pecks or probes at visible prey. It may also dig shallow pits to uncover food.
value.behavior: This plover is active and alert, often standing upright between short bursts of running. It commonly forages alone or in small groups but may roost with larger flocks of shorebirds. When disturbed, it may call sharply and fly with rapid wingbeats before settling elsewhere. On migration and in winter it uses open ground and shallow-water margins, where its mottled plumage provides effective camouflage. Individuals defend breeding territories and use distraction displays near nests and chicks.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although the species remains widespread and does not currently meet the criteria for a threatened category.
conservation.threats: Potential concerns include loss and degradation of coastal wetlands and other stopover or wintering habitats, disturbance at roosting and feeding sites, climate-driven changes in Arctic breeding conditions, and weather-related risks during long migrations.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect coastal mudflats, salt ponds, estuaries, and short-grass feeding areas used by migratory shorebirds. Limit disturbance near roosting flocks, keep dogs under control at important sites, support wetland conservation, and contribute well-documented observations to bird-monitoring programs such as eBird.
